title: Dumb Math Rules
subtitle: Pre-algebra and algebra fundamentals. Every rule carries its reason.

sections.title: The Grammar Nobody Teaches
sections.blurb: These are the unstated conventions the rest of math is built on. Most “I can't do algebra” is actually “nobody told me what the notation meant.”

rules.rule: `=` means “both sides weigh the same.” It is a scale, not “answer goes here.”
rules.why: Every legal move in algebra is just “keep the scale level” — that one idea generates all of solving.
rules.trap: On a calculator `=` means “go.” In algebra it never does.

rules.rule: **Term** = chunk separated by `+` or `−`. **Factor** = chunk separated by `×`. **Coefficient** = the number stuck to the front.
rules.why: Almost every rule cares which one you're looking at, and almost every mistake is treating a term like a factor.
rules.when: Before applying any rule, ask: am I looking at terms or factors?
rules.example: In `3x^2 + 5x`, there are 2 terms. In `3x^2`, the factors are 3, x, and x.

rules.rule: A number touching a letter means multiply. `3x` = `3 · x`. `2(x+1)` = `2 × (x+1)`.
rules.why: The × symbol looks exactly like the letter x, so mathematicians just stopped writing it.

rules.rule: **PEMDAS** — Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract.
rules.why: Multiplication is repeated addition, so it's the “bigger” operation and has to be collapsed into addition before you can add.
rules.trap: M and D are the **same rank** — do them left to right. Same for A and S. `8 ÷ 2 × 4 = 16`, not 1.
rules.mnemonic: Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally — but Mom & Dad are twins, and so are Aunt & Sally.

rules.rule: The minus sign has three different jobs: subtract (`5 − 3`), negative (`−3`), and opposite (`−x`).
rules.why: `−x` is not “a negative number” — it's “the opposite of whatever x is.” If x = −4, then −x = **4**.
rules.trap: This one trips up more people than anything else on this sheet.

sections.title: Negatives
sections.blurb: Think of −1 as an instruction: “flip to the other side of zero.” Everything here falls out of that.

rules.rule: Subtracting is adding the opposite. `a − b` = `a + (−b)`.
rules.why: It lets you stop tracking two different operations and just add signed numbers all day.
rules.when: Any time a string of +/− signs is confusing you, rewrite the whole thing as addition first.

rules.rule: Same signs: add and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract and take the sign of the bigger one.
rules.why: Same direction = piling up. Opposite directions = tug of war, and the stronger side wins.

rules.rule: Negative × negative = positive. Negative × positive = negative.
rules.why: ×(−1) means “flip across zero.” Flip twice and you're back where you started.
rules.mnemonic: Two wrongs make a right — but only in multiplication.

rules.rule: Distributing a negative flips **every** sign inside. `−(a − b)` = `−a + b`.
rules.why: That minus out front is really a `−1` multiplying each term separately.
rules.trap: Forgetting the second sign. `−(x − 5)` = `−x + 5`, not `−x − 5`.

rules.rule: `−x^2` and `(−x)^2` are different things.
rules.why: The exponent grabs tighter than the minus sign, so `−3^2` = `−(3^2)` = `−9`, but `(−3)^2` = `9`.
rules.when: If you want the negative squared, the parentheses are not optional.

sections.title: Fractions
sections.blurb: One idea unlocks this whole section: the bottom number is a NAME, not a quantity.

rules.rule: The denominator names the **size** of the piece. The numerator **counts** them.
rules.why: `3/4` is “three pieces, and the pieces are called fourths” — the 4 is a unit label, like “feet.”
rules.when: Every other fraction rule below is a consequence of this. When stuck, come back here.

rules.rule: Multiply straight across. `a/b × c/d` = `ac/bd`.
rules.why: Multiplying fractions is taking *a piece of a piece* — half of a third is a sixth, so the pieces get smaller and the names multiply.

rules.rule: Adding or subtracting needs a **common denominator** first.
rules.why: You can't count pieces of different sizes — same reason `3 feet + 2 meters` isn't 5 of anything until you convert.
rules.trap: `2/3 + 1/3 = 3/3`, not `3/6`. You're counting thirds; the name doesn't change.

rules.rule: Dividing = multiply by the reciprocal (flip the second one).
rules.why: “How many halves fit into 3?” is asking how many times you multiply up — so you flip and multiply.

rules.rule: You can cancel **factors**. You can never cancel **terms**.
rules.why: Canceling is secretly dividing top and bottom by the same thing, which only works if that thing is multiplying *everything*.
rules.trap: `(x+2)/2` is NOT `x`. But `2x/2` IS `x`.

rules.rule: `a/b = c/d`  →  `ad = bc` (cross-multiply).
rules.why: It isn't a trick — it's just multiplying both sides by b and then by d, and watching things cancel.
rules.when: Two fractions set equal to each other. Proportions, unit conversion, scaling recipes.

sections.title: Exponents
sections.blurb: An exponent is a tally of how many copies got written down. Every rule here is just counting them.

rules.rule: `x^a · x^b` = `x^{a+b}` — multiplying, so **add** the exponents.
rules.why: `x^2 · x^3` writes down 2 x's then 3 x's. Now count them: 5.
rules.trap: Only works when the base is the same. `x^2 · y^3` doesn't combine.

rules.rule: `x^a / x^b` = `x^{a-b}` — dividing, so **subtract**.
rules.why: Each x on the bottom cancels one on top. You're just counting the leftovers.

rules.rule: `(x^a)^b` = `x^{ab}` — power of a power, so **multiply**.
rules.why: b groups of (a copies of x). That's a·b copies.

rules.rule: `x^0 = 1`. Anything to the zero is 1.
rules.why: `x^3/x^3` is obviously 1, and the subtract rule says it's `x^0`. Both are true, so `x^0 = 1`.
rules.trap: It's 1, not 0. The 1 is the multiplicative starting point, the way 0 is for addition.

rules.rule: `x^{-a}` = `1/x^a`. A negative exponent means **flip it**, not “make it negative.”
rules.why: Walk the pattern down: 8, 4, 2, 1, ½, ¼. Each step down divides by 2 — nothing ever turns negative.

rules.rule: `x^{1/2}` = `√x`. A fractional exponent is a root.
rules.why: `x^{1/2} · x^{1/2} = x^1` by the add rule — so `x^{1/2}` is the thing that gives x when multiplied by itself. That's the square root.

rules.rule: `(ab)^n` = `a^n b^n`, but `(a+b)^n` is **NOT** `a^n + b^n`.
rules.why: Exponents distribute over multiplication only. `(2+3)^2 = 25`, while `2^2 + 3^2 = 13`.
rules.trap: This is the single most common algebra error there is. `(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2` — FOIL it, don't guess.

sections.title: Distributing & Factoring
sections.blurb: These are the same move run in opposite directions. Distributing takes parentheses apart; factoring puts them back.

rules.rule: `a(b + c)` = `ab + ac`
rules.why: 3 bags each holding (2 apples + 1 pear) gives you 6 apples and 3 pears. The 3 reaches everything inside.
rules.trap: It has to reach *every* term. `2(x + 3)` = `2x + 6`, not `2x + 3`.

rules.rule: **FOIL** — `(a+b)(c+d)` = `ac + ad + bc + bd`
rules.why: It's just distributing twice: every term on the left has to meet every term on the right.
rules.when: Two binomials multiplied. For anything bigger than 2×2 terms, forget FOIL and just make sure everything meets everything.

rules.rule: Combine like terms only: **same letter, same exponent**.
rules.why: `3x + 2x^2` is like `3 feet + 2 square feet` — different units, so it doesn't collapse.

rules.rule: Factor out the greatest common factor: `ab + ac` = `a(b + c)`
rules.why: Distribution running backwards. You're pulling the shared piece out front.
rules.when: First thing to try on any factoring problem, always.

rules.rule: Difference of squares: `a^2 − b^2` = `(a + b)(a − b)`
rules.why: FOIL it back: the two middle terms are `+ab` and `−ab`, which cancel.
rules.when: Two perfect squares with a minus between them. Recognize it on sight — it shows up constantly.

sections.title: Solving for x
sections.blurb: You are unwrapping a package. Whatever was wrapped last comes off first.

rules.rule: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
rules.why: The `=` is a balance scale. Change one pan without the other and it stops being true.

rules.rule: Undo operations in **reverse** PEMDAS order: A/S first, then M/D, then exponents, then parentheses.
rules.why: Wrapping a gift you go box → paper → ribbon. Unwrapping goes ribbon → paper → box. Solving is unwrapping.

rules.rule: To move something, do the **opposite** operation.
rules.why: `+` and `−` undo each other; `×` and `÷` undo each other. That's the only reason it works.
rules.trap: You're not “moving it to the other side and flipping the sign” — you're doing the same thing to both sides and one side cancels. Same result, but the second story is the one you can rebuild when you forget.

rules.rule: **Flip the inequality** when you multiply or divide by a negative.
rules.why: Multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, so bigger becomes smaller. `2 < 3`, but `−2 > −3`.
rules.trap: Only for × and ÷ by a negative. Adding or subtracting a negative doesn't flip anything.

rules.rule: Substitute your answer back in and check.
rules.why: It's the only step that catches a sign error, and sign errors are what actually cost you points.
Roots are just exponents in a hat — they distribute over multiplication only, same as every exponent rule.

rules.rule: Simplify by pulling out perfect-square factors. `√50` = `√(25·2)` = `5√2`.
rules.why: The multiply rule run backwards: split off the part that has a clean root and walk it out from under the radical.
The radical symbol means “the positive one.” `√((−3)^2)` = `√9` = `3`, not `−3`.

rules.rule: Percent means **per hundred**. `35%` = `35/100` = `0.35`.
rules.why: “cent” = hundred, same root as century and cents-per-dollar. A percent is always a fraction wearing a hat.

rules.rule: Decimal → percent: move the point 2 places **right**. Percent → decimal: 2 places **left**.
rules.why: That's multiplying or dividing by 100, which is the entire definition of percent.

rules.rule: “x% **of** y” means multiply.
rules.why: “Of” is the English word for multiplication. It never means anything else.

rules.rule: Percent change = `(new − old) / old`
rules.why: You're measuring the change against **where you started**, so the starting value always goes on the bottom.
rules.trap: Going 100 → 150 is +50%. Going 150 → 100 is −33%, not −50%. The denominator changed.

rules.rule: A ratio `a : b` is just the fraction `a/b`.
rules.why: Different notation, same object. If ratios feel hard, rewrite them as fractions and use the fraction rules.

sections.title: Functions & f(x) Notation
sections.blurb: A function is a machine: put a number in, get exactly one number out. Nearly all the difficulty here is notation, not concept.

rules.rule: `f(x)` does **not** mean f times x. It means "the machine f, applied to x."
rules.why: This is the one place in algebra where parentheses don't mean multiply — they mean "fed into."
rules.trap: You spent all of section #{distributing} learning that `2(x+1)` means multiply. `f(x+1)` does not. The rule changed and nobody said so.

rules.rule: `f(x)` and `y` are the same thing.
rules.why: Both name the output. `y = 2x + 1` and `f(x) = 2x + 1` are identical; the f version just tells you which machine made it.
rules.when: When a problem switches between them mid-question, nothing has changed. Keep going.

rules.rule: To find `f(3)`, replace **every** x with 3.
rules.why: x is a blank to be filled, not a value. The function is a recipe with a hole in it.

rules.rule: `f(x+1)` means put `x+1` into every blank. It is **not** `f(x) + 1`.
rules.why: Whatever sits in the parentheses is the input, however complicated it looks.

rules.rule: **Domain** = what you're allowed to put in. **Range** = what can come out.
rules.why: Only two things ever break a function at this level: dividing by zero, and even roots of negatives. Check for those and the domain is everything else.
rules.mnemonic: Domain is the Door (in). Range is the Result (out).

rules.rule: A graph is a function if no vertical line crosses it twice.
rules.why: One input must give exactly one output — two crossings means one x produced two y's, so it isn't a machine.

sections.title: The Coordinate Plane & Straight Lines
sections.blurb: This section pays off later: a regression line in statistics is exactly y = mx + b wearing different letters.

rules.rule: A point is `(x, y)` — always across first, then up.
rules.why: Alphabetical order, x before y. That's the whole reason; there isn't a deeper one.
rules.mnemonic: Into the house, then up the stairs.

rules.rule: Slope `m = rise / run = (y_2 - y_1) / (x_2 - x_1)`
rules.why: Slope is a rate: how much y changes for every 1 that x moves. Every other line rule follows from that one sentence.
rules.trap: Keep the points in the same order top and bottom. If y_2 came first, x_2 comes first too.

rules.rule: `y = mx + b` — m is the slope, b is where the line crosses the y-axis.
rules.why: Set x to 0: the `mx` term vanishes and you're left with `y = b`. So b is literally the value at the crossing.

rules.rule: Positive slope climbs left-to-right. Negative falls. Zero is flat. Vertical is **undefined**.
rules.why: It's rise over run: no rise gives 0, and no run gives division by zero, which isn't a number.
rules.trap: Zero slope and undefined slope are opposites, not synonyms. Flat line: `m = 0`. Vertical line: no m at all.

rules.rule: Parallel lines have the **same** slope. Perpendicular slopes are **negative reciprocals**.
rules.why: Turning a line 90° swaps rise and run and flips the direction — so `2/3` becomes `-3/2`.

rules.rule: To graph it: plot `b` first, then count the slope as rise-over-run to get the next point.
rules.why: b hands you one free point, and the slope is a set of directions from any point to another.

rules.rule: y-intercept: set `x = 0`. x-intercept: set `y = 0`.
rules.why: An intercept is where the *other* coordinate is zero — that's what touching an axis means.

sections.title: Systems of Equations
sections.blurb: Two equations, two unknowns. The answer is the one point that satisfies both — which on a graph is where the lines cross.

rules.rule: A solution must make **both** equations true at once.
rules.why: That's why the answer is the crossing point: it's the only place that sits on both lines.

rules.rule: **Substitution**: solve one equation for one variable, then put that into the other.
rules.why: It converts a two-unknown problem into a one-unknown problem, which you already know how to solve.
rules.when: Best when a variable is already alone, or has a coefficient of 1.

rules.rule: **Elimination**: add or subtract the two equations so one variable cancels.
rules.why: You're allowed to add equals to equals — both scales stay balanced, so the combined statement is still true.
rules.when: Best when the same variable has matching or opposite coefficients. Multiply one equation through to make that happen.

rules.rule: Variables all vanish? A **false** statement (`0 = 5`) means no solution. A **true** one (`0 = 0`) means infinitely many.
rules.why: No solution means the lines are parallel and never meet. Infinite means they're the same line drawn twice.
rules.trap: Getting `0 = 0` feels like you did something wrong. You didn't — it's an answer.

sections.title: Inequalities & Absolute Value
sections.blurb: Absolute value means distance from zero. Every rule here is that one idea applied to a number line.

rules.rule: `|x|` is the **distance** from zero, so it's never negative.
rules.why: Distance has no direction. Going 5 left and 5 right are both a trip of 5.

rules.rule: `|x| = 5` has **two** answers: `5` and `-5`.
rules.why: Both sit 5 units from zero, and the bars threw away which side you were on.
rules.trap: Losing the negative answer is the single most common absolute-value mistake.

rules.rule: `|x| < 5` means `-5 < x < 5` (a band). `|x| > 5` means `x < -5` **or** `x > 5` (two pieces).
rules.why: "Less than 5 away from zero" is the stretch around zero. "More than 5 away" is everything outside it.

rules.rule: Get the absolute value alone **before** you split it into two cases.
rules.why: The bars apply to whatever is inside them, so anything still stuck outside hasn't been dealt with yet.

rules.rule: Graphing: open circle for `<` and `>`, filled circle for `<=` and `>=`.
rules.why: Filled means the endpoint itself counts. Open means "up to here but not this."

rules.rule: Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative still flips it — see #{solving}.
rules.why: Same reason as before: multiplying by a negative mirrors the number line, so bigger becomes smaller.
rules.when: It applies inside absolute-value cases too, and that's where people forget it.

sections.title: Quadratics
sections.blurb: Anything with an `x^2`. It graphs as a parabola — a U — because squaring turns negatives positive, so the curve has to turn around.

rules.rule: **Zero Product Property**: if `A · B = 0`, then `A = 0` or `B = 0`.
rules.why: The only way to multiply to zero is for something to already be zero. This is the entire reason factoring solves equations.
rules.trap: It only works against **zero**. `A · B = 6` tells you nothing about A or B — get everything to one side first.

rules.rule: To factor `x^2 + bx + c`: find two numbers that **multiply to c** and **add to b**.
rules.why: It's FOIL backwards — the Last terms multiply to c, and the Outside plus Inside add to b.
rules.example: `x^2 + 5x + 6`: 2 and 3 multiply to 6, add to 5. So `(x+2)(x+3)`.

rules.rule: Quadratic formula: `x = (-b ± √(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a)`
rules.why: It's completing the square done once, in general, so nobody ever has to do it by hand again.
rules.when: When factoring doesn't work — which is most of the time outside a textbook.
rules.trap: The whole `-b ± √(b^2 - 4ac)` sits over `2a` — the `-b` included, not just the root.

rules.rule: `±` means work it twice: once with `+`, once with `-`.
rules.why: A square root has two answers, so the formula hands you both at once.

rules.rule: The discriminant `b^2 - 4ac` counts the real answers: positive → 2, zero → 1, negative → 0.
rules.why: It lives under the square root. A negative under a root has no real answer, so the parabola never crosses the x-axis.
rules.when: Useful when a question only asks *how many* solutions — you can skip the rest of the formula.

rules.rule: Get it to `ax^2 + bx + c = 0` before doing anything else.
rules.why: Both factoring and the formula assume one side is zero. Neither works otherwise.

sections.title: Rational Expressions
sections.blurb: Fractions with letters in them. There are no new rules here — section #{fractions} already covers all of it. The only new skill is factoring first.

rules.rule: Every fraction rule from #{fractions} applies unchanged. Letters change nothing.
rules.why: A fraction is a fraction. `x/y · a/b` multiplies straight across for exactly the same reason `1/2 · 1/3` does.

rules.rule: **Factor first, then cancel.** Never cancel before factoring.
rules.why: You can only cancel factors, never terms — and factoring is the operation that turns terms into factors.

rules.rule: The denominator can never be zero. Note which x values are banned.
rules.why: Division by zero is undefined, so those inputs are removed from the domain — even if they cancel away later.
rules.trap: In the example above, `x = -2` stays banned even though the `(x+2)` cancelled. The cancelling doesn't un-ban it.

rules.rule: Adding or subtracting still needs a common denominator — factor to find it.
rules.why: Same reason as numbers: you can't count pieces of different sizes. The factored form shows you what's missing.

sections.title: Scientific Notation
sections.blurb: Short section, but you will need it the moment you meet a p-value.

rules.rule: `a × 10^n`, where a is at least 1 and less than 10.
rules.why: Forcing exactly one digit before the decimal makes any two numbers instantly comparable by their exponent.

rules.rule: Positive exponent → big number. Negative exponent → small number.
rules.why: The exponent counts how many places the decimal moves, and negative exponents mean divide — see #{exponents}.
rules.example: `1.2 × 10^{-5}` is `0.000012`. That's a very small p-value.

rules.rule: Move the decimal `n` places: right for positive n, left for negative.
rules.why: Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one column up. Doing it n times shifts n columns.

sections.title: Word Problem Translation
sections.blurb: Word problems are a translation exercise, not a math exercise. Convert to symbols first, then solve.

rules.rule: **of** = `×` · **is / are / was** = `=` · **per / for each** = `÷` · **and / more than / sum** = `+` · **difference / less** = `−`
rules.why: These are fixed. They never mean anything else, which makes them the one part of word problems you can do mechanically.

rules.rule: “5 **less than** x” is `x − 5`. **Backwards from how you read it.**
rules.why: “Less than” and “more than” describe a change *to* the thing named after them, so that thing comes first.
rules.trap: This wording is chosen specifically to trip you up. Slow down every single time you see it.

rules.rule: Name the unknown out loud before you write anything. “Let x = the number of hours.”
rules.why: Half of word-problem failure is solving correctly for the wrong quantity. Writing the units down prevents it.
